name: Surgery-first orthognathic approach
lead: The surgery-first orthognathic approach (SFOA) is a way of sequencing corrective jaw surgery in which the bone operation is done before, or without, the traditional period of pre-surgical orthodontic treatment with braces. Conventional orthognathic care uses braces before and after surgery, with the pre-surgical phase traditionally lasting up to about a year.[11] For people seeking a change in facial structure through jaw surgery, the appeal described by surgeons and patients is that the new jaw position, and the facial change that comes with it, arrives at the start of treatment rather than after a year of braces.[3][4]

Orthognathic surgery reshapes the upper jaw (Le Fort I osteotomy), the lower jaw (sagittal split osteotomy), the chin (genioplasty) or combinations of these, and Wikipedia notes that it often produces a noticeable change in facial appearance.[11] In the surgery-first sequence, surgeons rely on 3D virtual planning and orthodontic miniscrews to control the bite afterwards, which they say allows stable occlusion without pre-surgical tooth decompensation.[1][2]

Studies, mostly in skeletal class III patients from East Asia and Europe, have compared SFOA with the conventional sequence on treatment time, stability, quality of life and accuracy.[2][3][8] The evidence base is mainly cohort and comparative studies, with a mix of findings, including reductions in total treatment time in some series and cautions about precautions and complications.[2][10] Within looksmaxxing culture it is discussed as a route for people hoping to reach jaw surgery results sooner, and users trade views on surgeons associated with the method.[13][14]
infobox: About 2-6 weeks initial healing; 2-4 further months for bone remodeling [11]

paras: Orthognathic surgery reshapes the jaws to treat bite, growth, airway and appearance problems and is usually done through the mouth.[11] One of the first published cases was by Simon Hullihen in 1849, jaw osteotomies were developed through the 1940s, and Hugo Obwegeser, born in 1920 and often called the father of modern orthognathic surgery, popularized the bilateral sagittal split osteotomy and refined the Le Fort I maxillary osteotomy; he presented his techniques to North American surgeons in 1966 and described combining upper and lower jaw surgery at the end of that decade.[11][16]

Traditionally, braces are worn before surgery to align the teeth over the jaws, and again afterwards to finish the bite. The pre-surgical phase can take up to a year, with retainers worn after braces come off.[11] Wikipedia estimates that roughly 5 percent of the US or UK population has a dentofacial deformity that needs surgery rather than braces alone.[11] Surgery-first and clear-aligner approaches are described as newer variations.[11]

In SFOA the surgeon moves the jaws to the planned position first, using a pre-planned surgical bite, and the orthodontist aligns and finishes the teeth afterwards. Because teeth are not pre-aligned, the planned surgical occlusion setup is central, and published work has described guidelines and accuracy of occlusal setups in class III correction.[9]

A 2009 editorial in the Journal of Clinical Orthodontics titled 'Surgery-first orthognathics' is among the early descriptions in the literature, and later cohorts from Asia and Europe reported experience with the method.[15][1]

A 2015 report from one surgical group describes adopting surgery-first without pre-surgical orthodontics for skeletal class III deformity, pointing to advances in pre-surgical orthodontic simulation and post-surgical miniscrew-assisted treatment that showed stability and control of the occlusion.[1] A 2017 prospective study framed the question as whether the approach can reduce total treatment time.[2]

Proponents of the approach also describe an earlier improvement in facial appearance, since the jaw is corrected at the start rather than after months of braces during which the bite can look worse.[3][4]

Virtual 3D planning is a central tool. A 2018 study compared 3D planning with actual outcomes in surgery-first cases,[7] and a Scientific Reports study described the characteristics and accuracy of surgical occlusion setups in class III correction using the approach.[9] A registered retrospective study is examining a tooth-bone dual-support osteotomy locating plate for accuracy and operation time in surgery-first treatment.[20]
A comparative study of postoperative stability after bilateral sagittal split ramus osteotomy for class III correction examined conventional surgery against surgery-first.[8]

A 2019 review, the second part of a series on the current status of the approach, discusses precautions and complications specific to surgery-first.[10] General orthognathic risks include bleeding, swelling, infection (reported up to 7 percent), nausea, and nerve injury with facial numbness, especially of the inferior alveolar nerve, which is usually temporary but rarely permanent.[11] Wikipedia adds that antibiotics given during surgery and continued for more than a day reduce infection risk.[11]

For orthognathic surgery in general, Wikipedia describes initial healing of about 2 to 6 weeks, with bone healing and remodeling taking a further 2 to 4 months; jaws may be immobilized for 1 to 4 weeks in some cases, patients typically follow a liquid diet at first and may lose weight, and swelling mostly resolves within weeks though some may last months.[11] Return to work is possible in 2 to 6 weeks.[11]

On looksmax.org, users discuss whether surgery-first is available for their bite, with one thread asking why proponents such as the surgeons named in the community offer it and whether it gives the same results as braces beforehand.[13] Members facing a year of pre-surgical braces describe the wait as frustrating and ask about bimaxillary surgery with a class III bite without it; others reply that decompensating the teeth before surgery matters for a class III bite.[13][14]
Posters also discuss the order of facial procedures. One user advises maxillary surgery before other facial procedures because it can change the mouth, nose and eye area.[17]

A 2017 prospective study investigated whether surgery-first reduces total treatment time compared with conventional treatment.[2] Two questionnaire-based studies compared oral health-related quality of life and satisfaction: one with 15 patients per arm[3] and one longitudinal study of 50 Chinese adults.[4] Psychological and biological aspects[5] and psychodynamic features[6] were compared between approaches in further cohort studies. Planning accuracy,[7] postoperative stability[8] and occlusal setup accuracy[9] have also been assessed.

Registered trials include a completed study of surgery-first in skeletal class III treatment (n=60, started 2022),[12] a study of surgery-first with aligners (recruiting, n=20),[18] and a retrospective study of a tooth-bone dual-support osteotomy locating plate in surgery-first treatment (n=20).[20] A 2026 controlled clinical study examined quality of life in class III patients treated with surgery-first using aligners or fixed appliances.[19] No large randomized trial results have been published.

timeline.event: Simon Hullihen publishes one of the first jaw-surgery cases.[11]
Hugo Obwegeser presents modern orthognathic techniques to North American surgeons.[16]
Raffaini introduces orthognathic surgery under local anesthesia with IV sedation, shortening recovery.[11]
Journal of Clinical Orthodontics editorial 'Surgery-first orthognathics'.[15]
Surgical group reports reliability of surgery-first without pre-surgical orthodontics in class III patients.[1]
Prospective study asks whether surgery-first reduces total treatment time; quality-of-life and stability comparisons published.[2][3][8]
Review of precautions and complications of the surgery-first approach (part II).[10]
Registered trials of surgery-first in class III and with aligners begin.[12][18]
Controlled clinical study of surgery-first with aligners versus fixed appliances published.[19]

lore.intro: Surgery-first comes up on looksmax.org among people planning bimaxillary surgery who want to avoid a year of braces and ask which surgeons will operate without them.[13][14]

claims.claim: Surgery-first lets you skip the year of braces before jaw surgery
claims.believers: Posters facing long pre-surgical braces ask whether surgeons who offer the approach can operate on an imperfect bite and get results comparable to braces first.[13]
claims.experts: Conventional care uses up to about a year of pre-surgical braces; a 2017 prospective study examined whether surgery-first reduces total treatment time, and braces are still used after surgery.[2][11]

claims.claim: The facial change shows up sooner
claims.believers: Proponents describe the jaw being corrected at the start of treatment rather than after months of braces.[3][4]
claims.experts: Quality-of-life and satisfaction questionnaire studies compared surgery-first with the traditional sequence.[3][4]

claims.claim: Surgery-first works for a class III bite with a recessed face
claims.believers: One poster asks whether a large genioplasty plus braces could replace bimax; another replies that decompensation is needed before surgery in class III.[14]
claims.experts: Most published comparisons of the approach are in skeletal class III patients, and a 2019 review covers precautions and complications.[8][10]

claims.claim: Jaw surgery should come before other facial surgery
claims.believers: One user advises maxillary surgery first because it can change the mouth, nose and eye area.[17]
claims.experts: No published studies in the cited research test the sequencing of jaw surgery against other facial procedures.

card.summary: Jaw surgery done before (or without) braces; studied in cohorts, with treatment-time and stability findings that vary by study.
card.note: Major jaw surgery; general orthognathic risks apply, plus planning-specific precautions.

quick.overview:
Surgery-first reorders corrective jaw surgery: the bone operation comes before, or replaces, the long pre-surgical braces phase. Surgeons using it say better 3D planning and miniscrews make this possible.

Studies, mostly cohort comparisons in class III patients, have looked at treatment time, stability, quality of life and planning accuracy.
quick.mechanism: The jaw is repositioned according to a virtual plan with a pre-set surgical bite, and orthodontic tooth movement follows afterwards, often with miniscrew assistance.
quick.risks: Orthognathic surgery carries risks of bleeding, swelling, infection and nerve injury with numbness that is usually temporary. A 2019 review discusses precautions and complications specific to the surgery-first sequence.

chain: Jaw repositioning is done first, guided by a 3D plan
Teeth are aligned with braces or aligners after surgery
Facial structure changes at the start of treatment instead of after months of braces
angle.text: Surgery-first changes the order of jaw surgery so that the skeletal change, such as a more forward upper or lower jaw or a corrected bite, happens earlier in treatment. People choosing it describe wanting the visible facial change and a shorter time in braces.
